<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? 
<br class="ltx_break">A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yi Shi
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tanyu Chen
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Kai Shen
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Continuum AI
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">research@orcarouter.ai</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Directional ablation removes an aligned language model’s ability to refuse by projecting a single “refusal direction” out of the weights that write the residual stream. It needs no gradient-based training and no optimization, only a few hundred contrastive prompts, which makes it the canonical white-box attack on open-weight alignment. However, it has been established only on dense models up to roughly 70B parameters. We study whether it survives the shift to frontier mixture-of-experts (MoE) models whose residual streams are no longer a single tensor and whose weights ship quantized. We apply it to GLM-5.3-Flash (320B parameters, 288 routed experts, a four-wide hyper-connection residual, block-FP8). The attack survives the architecture, but what it reaches is no longer where a reader of the original recipe would look for it. Editing the attention, dense and routed-expert writers on their own removes 0.039, 0.016 and 0.148 of refusal respectively; editing all three together removes 0.776. As a result, 74% of the effect exists only under the joint intervention. The part the conventional recipe reaches by module-name matching accounts for 0.066 of that 0.776, which is why it fails <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">silently</em> on an MoE. The effect does not follow from removing just any direction: ablating a random direction orthogonal to it leaves refusal unchanged. A category-concentrated residue survives every edit we tried: subspaces fitted on violence, sexual content and hate leave measurable refusal at every rank from 1 to 12. We report the method, the 41–89 percentage-point reductions it achieves across seven harmful benchmarks with no detected change in capability, and the boundary where it stops.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aligning a language model to refuse harmful requests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ganguli et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is, mechanistically, the installation of a behavior that a white-box adversary may later try to remove. The cheapest known removal is <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directional ablation</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>: refusal is mediated by a single linear direction in the residual stream, and orthogonalizing the weights that write that stream against the direction strips the behavior while leaving the model otherwise intact. It requires no gradient-based training, no optimization, and no access beyond the checkpoint itself. Anyone who can download an open-weight model can run it. This makes the geometry of refusal a security property of every released model rather than an academic curiosity. Yet the finding that refusal is a single direction was established on dense models up to roughly 70B parameters.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Frontier open weights have since diverged from the model this method assumes in three directions at once. Dense feed-forward blocks have become sparse mixtures of experts; the single residual stream has become the several parallel, per-layer-mixed streams of a hyper-connection residual; and the evidence that refusal is one direction, gathered on small models, has to carry to an untested frontier scale. Each divergence unsettles one of directional ablation’s premises. Sparsity unsettles the question of where to cut: the conventional recipe edits the dense projections and deliberately skips the router to preserve expert routing, but recent work locates safety-sensitive behavior inside the expert representations rather than in the routing decisions themselves <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and work extending steering to MoE models finds that the refusal signal it recovers does not coincide with expert routing at all, assigning a substantial role to attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marbut et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. A multi-stream residual unsettles how to cut at all, since hyper-connections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and their manifold-constrained variant mHC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> carry several parallel streams mixed per layer, and a projection applied to one stream has no obvious relation to what a later layer reads. Underneath both sits the single-direction hypothesis, established on dense models up to roughly 70B parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and since complicated by work that finds refusal mediated by several independent directions, or by an entire “concept cone” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wollschläger et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joad et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marshall et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which at frontier scale one direction may not capture. These premises matter operationally: a defender deploying open weights needs to know which part of the network the attack reaches, whether the recipes circulating online actually work at this scale, and how much of a model’s safety training is robust to removal at all.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We answer these questions on GLM-5.3-Flash, which exhibits all three shifts at once: 320B parameters, 288 routed experts (sparse), a four-wide hyper-connection residual (multi-stream topology), and block-FP8 weights (quantized). We apply directional ablation and document both what the method achieves and where it stops. Our subject is the <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">process</em>, not an evaluation of the model’s safety: where refusal lives in such a model, how the architecture and quantization must be handled, and the boundary the method reaches. The work is also instrumental: security research needs models that will engage with adversarial material, from malware behavior to exploitation logic to phishing patterns, and a model that refuses on surface features cannot support that analysis. Understanding what it takes to remove refusal, and what refuses to be removed, is therefore a prerequisite to building security tooling on open weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The premises do not fail alike, and the first to go is the assumption that refusal is written somewhere in particular. It has no answer at the level of a single group of weights: editing attention, the dense and shared projections, or the routed experts on their own removes 0.039, 0.016 and 0.148 of refusal, while editing all three together removes 0.776. Three quarters of the effect is not attributable to any group alone. What the conventional recipe reaches by module-name matching—attention and the dense projections—removes 0.066 of that 0.776, because the fused expert parameters are invisible to the module traversal it relies on; it reports a clean edit and changes almost nothing, which is what makes the failure silent. The multi-stream residual, by contrast, does not obstruct the attack: its mixing weights are scalar, so a direction that is zero in every stream stays zero, and editing the residual-writing weights turns out to be more thorough than hooking the layer output. The attack does not work by removing just any direction: ablating a random direction orthogonal to it leaves refusal where it was. Yet a fraction of refusal, concentrated in a few content categories, survives every subspace we fitted, up to rank 12. Across seven harmful benchmarks the method removes 41–89 percentage points of refusal with no detected change in capability. The width of that range is itself the boundary, since the benchmarks it clears least are the ones dense in the resistant categories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our contributions are:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We decompose the edit’s effect over all seven subsets of the writer groups in a 320B mixture-of-experts and find it strongly non-additive: no group removes much alone, and three quarters of the joint effect appears only when attention, the dense projections and the routed experts are edited together. The subset a name-matching implementation reaches removes 0.066 of an available 0.776, which is the silent-failure mode the conventional recipe hits on an MoE.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that directional ablation is compatible with a hyper-connection residual, and that editing the residual-writing weights is more thorough than hooking the layer boundary, a difference detected by a paired comparison on the same prompts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We empirically characterize the reach and limitations of the tested low-rank edits. The effect does not follow from removing an arbitrary direction: a random orthogonal direction removes nothing. But a category-concentrated residue survives subspaces fitted specifically on those categories at every rank from 1 to 12, and we report which categories they are.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Because the attack is already public and the checkpoint we study is uncensored, we defer threat model and release conditions to §<a href="#S6" title="6 Ethics and Responsible Release ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. There we argue that documenting where safety training is and is not robust to a known attack helps defenders more than it helps attackers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">That an aligned language model refuses harmful requests is a behavior acquired through safety training, and interpretability work has shown that this behavior is represented by low-dimensional linear structure in the residual stream <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wollschläger et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Directional ablation exploits exactly this: estimate one direction from a few hundred contrastive prompts, project it out of the weights that write the residual stream, and the behavior is gone, with no gradient steps and no optimization. The validity of that construction, however, rests on premises about how a model is built: that the residual stream is a single tensor, that the weights writing to it can be enumerated exhaustively, and that refusal is mediated by one linear direction within it. On the generation of models where the method was established, dense Transformers of at most roughly 70B parameters, these premises hold so naturally that they are rarely stated. Frontier open weights have since moved as a whole. Sparse mixtures of experts have replaced dense feed-forward blocks as the dominant route to scaling parameter count <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024</a>)</cite>. The residual stream has begun to be replaced by several parallel streams mixed layer by layer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Whether the premises still hold is no longer something that can be assumed.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Directional Ablation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Write the residual stream at layer <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> take the refusal direction to be the difference in means between harmful and harmless prompts over the last-token representation at some layer, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=\mathbb{E}_{\text{harmful}}[h^{l}_{-1}]-\mathbb{E}_{\text{harmless}}[h^{l}_{-1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mtext>harmful</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mtext>harmless</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=\mathbb{E}_{\text{harmful}}[h^{l}_{-1}]-\mathbb{E}_{\text{harmless}}[h^{l}_{-1}]</annotation></semantics></math>, normalized to unit length. To remove refusal, every weight matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> that writes to the residual stream—the embedding matrix <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> together with the attention output projections <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{O}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{O}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and the feed-forward down-projections <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{down}}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>down</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{down}}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, which are where a feed-forward block writes its output back <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geva et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, at each layer—is replaced by <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W\leftarrow W-rr^{\top}W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W\leftarrow W-rr^{\top}W</annotation></semantics></math>, which projects each writer’s output onto the orthogonal complement of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>; thereafter the direction <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is never written into the stream. The operation needs no gradients and no optimization, only the prompts the two means are taken over. On dense open-weight models of up to roughly 70B parameters it removes refusal at negligible cost to capability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The simplicity of the method, however, conceals how much it assumes about the architecture. The construction above is correct only under three premises, which the original work does not state explicitly because a dense Transformer supplies them directly. <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(i) The writers can be enumerated exhaustively</span>: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> together with <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{W_{O}^{l},W_{\text{down}}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>down</mtext><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{W_{O}^{l},W_{\text{down}}^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> are all of the residual stream’s writers, fixed in number and in one-to-one correspondence with module names. <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(ii) The residual is a single additive channel</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2021</a>)</cite>: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{l+1}=h^{l}+f(h^{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{l+1}=h^{l}+f(h^{l})</annotation></semantics></math>, so every writer’s output is added into the same tensor, and eliminating <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> at the writing end is therefore equivalent to eliminating it at any downstream read. <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(iii) Refusal is mediated by a single direction</span>: a rank-one projection suffices to remove the behavior. Premise (iii) is empirical, and its scope extends only as far as the models on which it has been tested; (i) and (ii) are structural, and hold as long as the architecture does not change. Two recent changes in frontier open weights, however, each alter one of them.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Sparse Mixtures of Experts</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models scale parameter count through conditional computation: the feed-forward block at each layer is replaced by <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> experts <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{f_{e}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{f_{e}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, of which a router <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> selects the top-<math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> per token, giving <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{e\in\mathrm{TopK}}g_{e}(x)f_{e}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>TopK</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{e\in\mathrm{TopK}}g_{e}(x)f_{e}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shazeer et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fedus et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024</a>)</cite>. Current frontier open-weight models favor fine-grained experts, with <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> in the hundreds and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> in the single digits, together with a shared expert that is always active for every token <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. GLM-5.3-Flash instantiates this design with <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E=288" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>288</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E=288</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=8</annotation></semantics></math>, and one shared expert.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the model, this change concerns only capacity and compute efficiency; for directional ablation, however, it changes what premise (i) ranges over. Each expert’s down-projection <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{down}}^{l,e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mtext>down</mtext><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{down}}^{l,e}</annotation></semantics></math> adds its output directly into the residual stream and is therefore a writer in its own right, so the feed-forward writers at each layer go from one to <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E+1</annotation></semantics></math>. The growth in count is by itself manageable: enumerating <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E+1</annotation></semantics></math> matrices is no different in kind from enumerating one. What differs is how they are stored. To be executed efficiently through a grouped GEMM, mainstream implementations stack a layer’s <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> expert weights into a single three-dimensional tensor of shape <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[E,d_{\text{ff}},d]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mtext>ff</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[E,d_{\text{ff}},d]</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gale et al., 2023</a>)</cite> rather than keeping <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> separate linear layers. Public ablation implementations collect writers by traversing modules and matching on names such as <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">down_proj</span>, which is sufficient whenever (i) is guaranteed by the architecture; fused experts, however, appear neither under that name nor as linear layers at all, so when the traversal finishes they are simply absent from the writer set, and nothing raises an error. A procedure that is correct on a dense model will therefore skip the overwhelming majority of an MoE’s feed-forward parameters without emitting any signal that it has done so. How much it thereby misses depends on a question that never had to be answered before: how much of refusal is written by the experts, and how much by the attention and dense projections.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Multi-Stream Residuals</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The residual stream is the least-revised component of the Transformer: since ResNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016</a>)</cite> it has been a single additive chain, and premise (ii) follows from precisely that. Hyper-connections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> are the first substantive generalization of the design: the residual becomes <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> parallel streams <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi>l</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, a layer reads a weighted combination of the streams as its input, writes its output back into them under learned weights, and an <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\times n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\times n</annotation></semantics></math> mixing matrix acts across streams at every layer. Manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> further constrain that mixing matrix to the manifold of doubly stochastic matrices, which is what makes the design stable to train at frontier scale. GLM-5.3-Flash adopts mHC with <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=4</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For training this generalization is a gain; for ablation, however, it removes the one structure premise (ii) depends on. The claim that eliminating <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> at the writing end also eliminates it at the reading end holds because nothing but element-wise addition sits between the two. (This is not the same as saying that editing the writers and projecting at the layer output are interchangeable: within a layer, a sublayer can read an intermediate state that a boundary projection has not yet reached. We return to that in §<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablation under a Multi-Stream Residual ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>.) Under multiple streams, a writer’s output is distributed across <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> streams, those streams are recombined by the mixing matrix at every layer, and what a layer reads is the combination. This does not mean that ablation must fail. But whether a projection at the writing end still guarantees an <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>-free read now depends on the form of the mixing operator. If it acts only on the stream index, weighting each stream’s <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector by a scalar, then any linear combination of streams still has zero component along <math id="S2.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>; if it acts non-trivially within the hidden dimension, it does not. This is decidable directly from the operator’s definition, yet to our knowledge no prior work has examined it in the context of ablation. And even where the answer is favorable, the multi-stream residual leaves a second question open. Writer-level and layer-boundary projections need not be equivalent even in a single-stream Transformer, because a sublayer can read an intermediate state before a boundary projection is applied. Whether multi-stream mixing widens that discrepancy has to be measured rather than argued.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Linear representations of refusal and weight editing.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al. (2024)</a></cite> show across thirteen open-weight chat models of up to 72B parameters that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace of the residual stream, and give two ways to exploit it. One is an inference-time activation intervention along that direction, of a kind developed more broadly as activation steering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Turner et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panickssery et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023a</a>)</cite>; the other is a white-box jailbreak that orthogonalizes the residual-writing weights against it. The premise both rest on is that features occupy linear directions in representation space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and the weight-editing form places the method alongside other direct interventions on parameters, such as locating and rewriting factual associations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, arithmetic on task vectors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and low-rank adaptation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. The latter changes nothing about inference and adds no overhead, since once the edit is applied the model deploys like any other, and it has accordingly become the most widely circulated way to uncensor open weights. Reproductions and much of the work that followed, however, inherit the original recipe without revisiting the architectural conditions it depends on: how the writers are enumerated, and what topology carries the residual, were supplied directly by the dense models the recipe was developed on, and so never became things that had to be discussed. Whether the recipe still holds once a model stops supplying those conditions has not been tested.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Other ways to remove safety behavior.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Prompt-level jailbreaks leave the weights alone and search for an input that evades the trained behavior, whether by gradient-guided suffix optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, by exploiting the mismatch between capability and safety training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, or by collecting prompts that already circulate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2024</a>)</cite>; the behavior survives in the model and each new request must defeat it again. Fine-tuning removes it from the weights instead, and does so cheaply: ten adversarially designed examples suffice on a hosted model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, a hundred malicious examples and an hour of GPU time suffice on open weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and a quantized low-rank adapter fitted on one GPU for under $200 brings a 70B chat model’s refusal rate to roughly one percent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lermen et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Directional ablation sits below both in cost. It needs no optimization against the model and no gradient step at all, only a forward pass over a few hundred prompts, which is why it is the recipe that circulates for open weights and the one whose reach at frontier scale is worth measuring.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Linear concept erasure.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Removing a direction from a representation is a general operation with its own literature. Iterative nullspace projection removes a protected attribute by repeatedly projecting out the directions a linear probe finds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ravfogel et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and LEACE gives the closed-form projection that erases a concept while perturbing the representation as little as possible <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Belrose et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. That line works on activations and asks what a probe can still recover; the weight-editing form used here asks instead what behavior survives, and it inherits the assumption those methods established: that the concept occupies a low-dimensional linear subspace, estimated in practice by a difference of class means <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marks and Tegmark, 2024</a>)</cite>, over features that superposition packs into a space smaller than their number <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Elhage et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Refusal ablation is that construction applied to one behavior and pushed through to the weights.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">How deep safety training goes.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A recurring finding is that alignment is thin. Instruction tuning on a thousand curated examples recovers most of it <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and safety behavior in particular concentrates in the first few generated tokens, which is why prefilling an answer defeats it and why fine-tuning undoes it so cheaply <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Unlearning aims at the opposite property, removing a capability from the weights rather than gating it <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and tamper-resistant safeguards aim at making a safety property survive an adversary who holds the weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tamirisa et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Where a weight edit reaches, and what it fails to reach, is the measurement those defenses would have to be evaluated against.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Geometry beyond a single direction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Later work has refined the representational picture. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wollschläger et al. (2025)</a></cite> find refusal mediated not by one direction but by a multi-dimensional “concept cone” whose directions are representationally independent. Other work recovers geometrically distinct directions for each of eleven refusal categories, yet reports that they yield nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, differing mainly in <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how</em> the model refuses rather than whether it does <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Joad et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Refusal has also been characterized as an affine rather than a purely linear function <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marshall et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Together these results point to the single-direction account being incomplete. What they characterize, however, is the geometry of the representation, largely through analysis and steering in activation space and largely on dense models of at most roughly 70B parameters. How much refusal a single rank-one weight edit actually removes at frontier scale is a question at a different level. That several directions exist in the representation and that removing several directions removes more refusal are not the same claim; whether the second holds has not been established at this scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Safety in mixture-of-experts models.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As MoE architectures have become standard, recent work has begun to ask how safety behavior is distributed over the experts. RASET <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> reports that routing in aligned MoE models is largely topic-driven, identifies safety-critical experts by a contrastive routing-sensitivity criterion, and alters their behavior by parameter-efficient tuning of those experts alone, leaving the routing path intact. Work extending steering to MoE models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marbut et al., 2026</a>)</cite> exploits refusal-related expert routing patterns and expert-specific steering directions. It reports that the refusal signal the steering recovers does not coincide with expert routing behavior, which it reads as evidence that attention plays a substantial role in MoE refusal. This work establishes that experts and safety behavior are connected, but these interventions either require gradient-based tuning or operate on activations at inference time; neither provides the training-free weight edit studied here. Whether a training-free, gradient-free weight edit succeeds turns instead on a quantity that has not been measured: which parameters write refusal into the residual stream, and how much of that writing falls to the experts as against the attention and dense projections.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architectural changes to the residual stream.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hyper-connections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and their manifold-constrained variant mHC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>)</cite> replace the single residual with several parallel streams and mix across them at every layer, motivated by training stability and representation quality. As architecture papers they are evaluated on perplexity and downstream task performance, which is the appropriate standard for what they set out to do. Representation-level interventions—activation patching, steering vectors, and the weight orthogonalization used here—rest on the premise that the residual is a single additive channel, and that premise is exactly what the multi-stream design alters. To our knowledge no prior work has examined whether these interventions remain valid under a multi-stream residual, nor where within such a structure an edit should be applied.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method and Setup</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To probe how far a single direction reaches, we keep the recipe fixed and change the model. The direction is still one unit vector given by the difference of means over harmful and harmless prompts, and the edit is still one rank-one projection applied to every weight that writes into the residual stream. No training, no gradients, and no second direction are introduced. The target model, however, is chosen outside the conditions the recipe was developed under: a sparse mixture of experts of roughly 320B parameters, a residual carried by four parallel streams, and weights released in block-FP8. The recipe touches this architecture at three points: enumerating the writers inside fused expert tensors, reading activations from several residual streams, and orthogonalizing quantized codes. At each we do only what is needed for the recipe to apply at all, and measure the loss that the handling itself introduces. Whatever difference remains in the results can then be attributed to the single direction rather than to engineering workarounds.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Target Model and the Writer Set</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GLM-5.3-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Z.ai, 2026</a>)</cite>, the latest of the GLM family <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, exhibits all three features at once, which is why it serves as the entry point. It is a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 320B total and 18B active parameters: 45 Transformer layers plus one multi-token-prediction (MTP) module <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gloeckle et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, hidden size 4096; hybrid attention, with 34 gated linear layers implementing Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team, 2025</a>)</cite> and 11 multi-head latent attention (MLA) layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2024</a>)</cite> running sparse full attention, the latter with a top-2048 indexer in the manner of DeepSeek sparse attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a>)</cite>; 288 routed experts per layer under top-8 routing plus one shared expert, the first three layers being dense MLPs; a four-stream manifold-constrained hyper-connection residual; and a native vision and video tower. The weights are released in block-FP8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Micikevicius et al., 2022</a>)</cite> (e4m3, <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128\times 128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128\times 128</annotation></semantics></math> blocks) across 62 shards and 76,108 tensors. Frontier open weights now ship quantized as a matter of course, whether in a narrow float format or under a post-training scheme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dettmers et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frantar et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, so a weight edit has to be applied to codes rather than to matrices — a condition none of the published ablation recipes addresses. The parameter counts above include the 7.4B MTP module and the 0.56B vision tower.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Matrices that write into the language residual stream of GLM-5.3-Flash: 12,442 in FP8 and 37 in BF16. Counting is at the level of weight matrices; the 12,442 block scale tensors that the requantization updates alongside them are not separate writers.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The criterion for a writer is a single one: a matrix whose output is added directly into the language residual stream. Enumerating exhaustively under this criterion gives 12,479 matrices (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.1 Target Model and the Writer Set ‣ 4 Method and Setup ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), of which 12,442 are stored in FP8 and 37 in BF16: 34 attention output projections on the gated-linear layers, the token embedding, the MTP input projection and the vision merger. Comparing the released edited checkpoint against the base tensor by tensor confirms the inventory from the artifact rather than from the code: 24,921 of the 76,108 tensors differ, being exactly these 12,479 weight matrices and the 12,442 block scale tensors that the requantization updates with them, and nothing else moved. The router, the two reader projections (gate and up), all hyper-connection mixers, the sparse-attention indexer, the normalization layers, and the unembedding do not write into the residual and are left unchanged. The expert down-projections account for 99.2% of all writers; they exist as three-dimensional fused tensors, and they are exactly what matching on module names fails to reach.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Estimating the Direction and Choosing the Layer</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Direction estimation follows the original recipe. Harmful prompts are drawn from AdvBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2023b</a>)</cite> and harmless prompts from the Alpaca instructions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Taori et al., 2023</a>)</cite> that carry no context input; each is split into two disjoint sets, 256 and 256 for estimating the direction and 32 and 32 for choosing the layer. A further 64 prompts each from the harmful and benign splits of JailbreakBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> serve as a held-out test from a source different from the fitting data. For every layer we take the residual representation at the last token, subtract its mean over the harmless set from its mean over the harmful set, and normalize to a unit vector, computing throughout in float32.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The estimator carries one safeguard: dimensions whose mean magnitude exceeds ten times the layer <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">median</em> are masked before the difference is taken, because a handful of content-independent dimensions with an order-of-magnitude larger activation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite> would otherwise dominate it. <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">On this checkpoint the safeguard never fires.</span> At layer 22, where the direction is fitted, no dimension exceeds the threshold: masking at ten times the median and not masking at all produce the same vector to the last bit, so the direction reported here is the raw difference of means.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Sweeping the multiplier shows the setting is not a tuned one (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Estimating the Direction and Choosing the Layer ‣ 4 Method and Setup ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). Tightening it damages the direction: at a multiplier of 2 it masks 558 of 4096 dimensions, turns the direction to a cosine of 0.898 against the shipped one, and leaves refusal at 0.691 where the shipped direction leaves 0.156. A multiplier of 5 masks two dimensions and leaves refusal at 0.133, below 0.156 by less than the run-to-run variation of greedy decoding under tensor parallelism, which we do not read as an improvement. The sweep was run at layer 22 only.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T2.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Multiplier</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Dims masked</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><math id="S4.T2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>cos</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos</annotation></semantics></math> to shipped</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Refusal</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T2.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">2</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">558</th>
<td id="S4.T2.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.898</td>
<td id="S4.T2.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.691</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">3</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">107</th>
<td id="S4.T2.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.977</td>
<td id="S4.T2.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.227</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T2.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T2.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">5</th>
<th id="S4.T2.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">2</th>
<td id="S4.T2.2.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.9987</td>
<td id="S4.T2.2.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.133</td></tr>

<th id="S4.T2.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0</th>

<th id="S4.T2.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0</th>
<td id="S4.T2.2.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">1.0000</td>

</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Massive-activation mask at layer 22, swept over the multiplier of the layer median. Refusal is measured on the 256 held-out harmful prompts with all writers hooked.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Layer selection is done on the validation set. Nine candidate layers between depth 0.4 and 0.8 are each ablated at inference time through a hook that subtracts the layer’s direction, with the weights untouched, and scored by the bypass rate on harmful prompts minus a KL penalty on harmless prompts, the latter keeping the edit from spilling into ordinary behavior. Layer 22 (depth 0.49) scores highest. Layers 20 and 22 are effective while layer 25 is not; this non-monotonicity reproduces stably on the validation set and is not measurement noise, so the layer has to be measured rather than set from a depth fraction.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Applying the Edit under Fused Experts and a Multi-Stream Residual</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The original recipe assumes that writers can be found by module name and that the residual can be read as a single tensor. This model satisfies neither.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Writers are collected by traversing the structure of the parameter tensors rather than by matching names. A three-dimensional expert tensor is unfolded along its first dimension into one two-dimensional matrix per expert, and these enter the writer set alongside the ordinary linear layers. The step involves no algorithmic difficulty, but it decides whether the edit lands on the weights that actually write the residual.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The multi-stream residual affects reading but not editing. When activations are read, a layer’s residual is a bundle of shape <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[B,S,4,H]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[B,S,4,H]</annotation></semantics></math>; it is collapsed into a single <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector under the hyper-connection’s mixing weights before the last-token representation is taken. Applying the edit requires nothing further. The cross-stream mixing in mHC weights each stream as a whole by a scalar and performs no rotation within the hidden dimension, so a direction that is zero in every stream remains zero after mixing. The edit is applied, as in the original recipe, to the writer weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The edit ultimately has to land in the checkpoint on disk, and this checkpoint cannot be edited in memory and saved back, for three independent reasons: the weights are FP8 codes rather than real matrices, and projecting the codes directly destroys the matrix; the experts are fused into three-dimensional parameters at load time; and <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transformers</span> drops the MTP module (<span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">layers.45</span>) on loading, so that <span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">save_pretrained</span> silently writes 6.98 GiB less than it read. We therefore stream each shard in, rewrite it, and write it back, and after editing verify that all 62 shards and 76,108 tensors match the base checkpoint in name, dtype, and shape.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Applying the Edit to Block-FP8 Weights</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The rank-one projection is defined on real matrices, while the weights are stored as codes. A block-FP8 matrix consists of e4m3 codes and a per-block scale (<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">weight_scale_inv</span>) holding one coefficient per <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128\times 128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128\times 128</annotation></semantics></math> block. The edit therefore proceeds in three steps: dequantize under the per-block scales, project in float32, requantize, and write back both the codes and the updated scales. Two errors here leave no visible trace afterwards. The scales must be written back in the dtype the checkpoint uses: narrowing an fp32 scale to bf16 discards 16 mantissa bits, changes the file size, and may bypass the branch a loader dispatches on <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scale.dtype</span>. And quantization must use the very scale that is written to the file; otherwise an avoidable layer of error is introduced between the codes and the scales.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T3.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T3.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt">Iterations</th>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt">Residual leakage</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt">Weight perturbation</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t">8</th>
<td id="S4.T3.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t">13.4%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t">2.15%</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T3.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb">32</th>
<td id="S4.T3.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">5.2%</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb">2.79%</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Iterated orthogonalization under block-FP8 requantization, measured on one MLA output projection with the same direction.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More fundamental than either is that requantization reintroduces part of the component that was just projected out. Measured on a real MLA output projection with the same direction, a single project–quantize–dequantize round leaves a substantial residue; repeating the cycle lets each round clean up the rounding error of the previous one, and the residue falls with the number of iterations while the weight perturbation rises (Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Applying the Edit to Block-FP8 Weights ‣ 4 Method and Setup ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When only attention is edited this leakage is negligible: 34 of the 45 writers at that stage are BF16 with about 1% leakage, and the leakage of the remaining 11 FP8 matrices is lost in the noise, a lossless hook giving a refusal rate of 0.812 against 0.828 after baking. When all writers are edited, however, 12,442 FP8 matrices are involved and the leakage accumulates matrix by matrix: the lossless hook predicts a refusal rate of 0.031, while the model baked with 8 iterations gives 0.188. Raising the iteration count to 32 lowers the leakage from 13.4% to 5.2% and the refusal rate from 0.188 to 0.094, recovering about half of the gap. Beyond that the leakage falls slowly while the weight perturbation keeps growing, so we take 32 as the operating point. The measured maximum residual leakage after editing is 0.149 for FP8 and 0.024 for BF16.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Evaluation Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluation covers three kinds of behavior: refusal on harmful prompts, over-refusal, and general capability; the benchmarks, sample sizes, and scoring rules are listed in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Benchmarks. ‣ 4.5 Evaluation Setup ‣ 4 Method and Setup ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. There are seven harmful benchmarks, each sampled from its full set under a fixed random seed. Over-refusal uses the 250 safe prompts of XSTest, which carry sensitive surface features but are harmless, so that refusing them is a false refusal. The before-and-after comparison shows whether what the edit removes is the harmful part of refusal or the harmless part along with it. The four capability benchmarks are multiple-choice tasks scored by the logit of the first token of each option letter, except GSM8K, which keeps chain-of-thought generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2022</a>)</cite> because it needs the reasoning. Base and edited models run under identical settings: greedy decoding, the same random seed, <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">reasoning_effort=low</span>, with <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;think&gt;</span> blocks stripped before classification. Every response is logged in full, so re-judging, paired tests, and per-category breakdowns need no regeneration.</p>
</div>
