</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Evaluation benchmarks. <em id="S4.T4.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Overlap</em> is the fraction of a benchmark’s sample that falls on the AdvBench prompts used to estimate the direction; the three non-zero entries each have a clean variant drawn only from outside the fitting slice. MMLU-Pro is scored by letter logit and is therefore lower than a chain-of-thought run of the same benchmark; it serves only for the before-and-after comparison and is not comparable to absolute figures reported elsewhere.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Judge.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A rule-based classifier that checks only whether the response opens with a fixed phrase misses empathetic refusals: under a self-harm prompt, “I’m worried about you… please reach out to…” is an unambiguous refusal that contains no template phrase. We instead re-judge every logged response with a judge model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> from a different model family (DeepSeek-v4-flash), blind, cached, and retried with back-off on failure; the different family also avoids self-judging. The two judgments agree on 0.85–0.96 of responses on the harmful benchmarks, and the disagreement is systematic in direction: the rule-based classifier underestimates refusal on harmful sets. The main text reports the judge model’s figures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The judge returns one of three labels, <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span> and <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span>, and which of them count as refusal has to be stated rather than assumed. Scoring everything that is not <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span> as refusal folds in replies that ran out of the token budget; on harmful prompts that is 0–9 items per condition and changes little, but on harmless prompts 21 of 100 base-model replies were cut off, which would report a 0.260 false-refusal rate for a model that actually refuses 5 of the 100. We therefore count only <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span> as refusal throughout, report the alternative as a <em id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">non-compliance rate</em> where it is informative, and give the label counts for every condition in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> (Tables <a href="#A1.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>, <a href="#A1.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, <a href="#A1.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> and <a href="#A1.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>). Items for which the judge returned no usable verdict after retries are excluded and the affected <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is stated.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contamination.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The direction is fitted on AdvBench, and the evaluation also samples AdvBench. Under the same random seed, all 100 prompts of that benchmark fall on the fitting data, and JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT each share a small number of prompts with AdvBench in wording. For these three benchmarks we construct clean variants using only samples outside the fitting slice, and every claim about generalization rests on the clean variants.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Statistics.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rates are reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilson, 1927</a>)</cite>. A percentile bootstrap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Efron, 1979</a>)</cite> degenerates where a rate sits at the boundary: 50 successes out of 50 returns <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1.000,1.000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1.000,1.000]</annotation></semantics></math> against Wilson’s <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.929,1.000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.929</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.929,1.000]</annotation></semantics></math>, and several rates here do sit there, so Wilson is what we quote. The paired capability comparison, whose statistic is a difference rather than a rate, uses a paired bootstrap over items <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Efron, 1979</a>)</cite>. The key pairwise comparisons are made on the same set of prompts with McNemar’s paired test <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">McNemar, 1947</a>)</cite>, which is more sensitive than an unpaired comparison and does not mistake variance between prompts for a difference between conditions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Infrastructure.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model is loaded with <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">transformers</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al., 2020</a>)</cite> under tensor parallelism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shoeybi et al., 2019</a>)</cite> with expert parallelism (TP8+EP). One detail of distributed generation cost us several runs before we found it: every rank must execute the same number of decode steps. <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">generate</span> decides when to stop from the sequences it can see, and that decision is rank-local, so a rank that stops one step early leaves the others waiting on a collective that is never issued, and the job deadlocks with every GPU allocated and idle. We caught it in the NCCL flight recorder as rank 0 reducing a <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[8,4096]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[8,4096]</annotation></semantics></math> decode step while ranks 1–7 reduced the <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[856,4096]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>856</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4096</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[856,4096]</annotation></semantics></math> prefill of the next batch at the same collective sequence number. Passing <span id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">synced_gpus</span> keeps the loop running on every rank until all of them are done and removes the hang; a short watchdog timeout only shortens the wait for a deadlock that should not occur. Long stages additionally checkpoint per condition so that an interrupted run resumes rather than restarts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The edited model’s refusal rate on seven harmful benchmarks falls from 0.51–1.00 to 0.08–0.48, no capability score moves detectably, and false refusal on harmless prompts drops to zero. A single direction removes most of this model’s refusal. The size of the reduction, however, differs by a factor of two across benchmarks, the residue ranges from 0.08 to 0.48, and the confidence intervals at the two ends do not overlap, so the spread is not noise. §<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> gives the full safety and capability results and identifies which benchmarks the spread falls on. The four subsections that follow each take up one question: §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Which Weights the Edit Needs ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> measures every subset of the writer groups under lossless hooks; §<a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Ablation under a Multi-Stream Residual ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a> derives what the mHC mixing operator guarantees and compares editing the writers against projecting at the layer boundary; §<a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 What the Edit Is Specific To ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a> asks whether the effect is specific to the direction removed and whether a second direction changes it; and §<a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a> breaks the residue down by content category and fits subspaces on the resistant categories at every rank from 1 to 12.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">

<td id="S5.T5.2.9.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">0.152 [0.094, 0.235]</td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><math id="S5.T5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.84" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.84</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.84</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><math id="S5.T5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{\times}10^{-25}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{\times}10^{-25}</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T5.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T5.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">JailbreakBench (clean)</td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right">92</td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">0.946 [0.879, 0.977]</td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left">0.196 [0.127, 0.288]</td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.10.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right"><math id="S5.T5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-0.75" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.75</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.75</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>Harmful refusal and false refusal, judged by the judge model and counting only <span id="S5.T5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. <math id="S5.T5.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of prompts with a usable verdict on both checkpoints; one AdvBench response has none, so those rows are scored out of 99. Per-condition label counts are in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> gives refusal rates on the seven harmful benchmarks and the three clean variants. The base model refuses 0.92–1.00 on six of them; ForbiddenQuestions is the exception at 0.51, because a substantial share of its questions are sensitive rather than harmful and the base model answers them. After editing, the seven rates lie between 0.08 and 0.48, and every reduction is significant under a paired McNemar test (<math id="S5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;10^{-7}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;10^{-7}</annotation></semantics></math> throughout; the prompts are paired within each benchmark, 50 to 150 of them). The discordant pairs run almost entirely in one direction. Across the seven harmful benchmarks, 799 prompts carry a usable verdict on both checkpoints; 546 of them are refused by the base model and not by the edited one—537 becoming compliant answers and 9 running out of the token budget—while two move the other way, one on StrongREJECT and one on ForbiddenQuestions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report Wilson intervals rather than bootstrap ones. The two disagree where a rate sits at the boundary, which several of these do: a percentile bootstrap of 50 successes out of 50 returns <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[1.000,1.000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[1.000,1.000]</annotation></semantics></math> against Wilson’s <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.929,1.000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.929</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.929,1.000]</annotation></semantics></math>, a gap of 0.071 at the lower bound, and 0 out of 250 gives <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.000,0.000]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.000</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.000,0.000]</annotation></semantics></math> against <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.000,0.015]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.000</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.015</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.000,0.015]</annotation></semantics></math>. Wilson does not degenerate at the boundary, so it is the interval we quote throughout.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The clean variants give figures close to the contaminated originals: 0.152 against 0.131 on AdvBench, 0.196 against 0.150 on JailbreakBench, 0.327 against 0.380 on StrongREJECT. All three differences fall inside the confidence intervals and do not even agree in sign. The direction was estimated from 256 AdvBench prompts, and the edited model falls just as far on prompts it never saw, so what was removed is not memorization of the fitting sample. Every claim about generalization below rests on the clean variants.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The edit did not make the model more cautious on harmless prompts; it did the opposite. The 250 safe XSTest prompts carry sensitive surface features, the base model falsely refuses six of them, and the edited model refuses none.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>Capability, paired item by item. Both checkpoints answer the same items in the same order, so the comparison is paired and the interval is a paired bootstrap over items. McNemar gives <math id="S5.T6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.63" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.63</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.63</annotation></semantics></math> on MMLU and <math id="S5.T6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.00</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=1.00</annotation></semantics></math> on the other three, with near-symmetric flips (10:7, 10:11, 1:2, 7:8).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Capability is given in Table <a href="#S5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Every paired interval straddles zero, no test is significant, and the items that change answer do so in both directions in near-equal numbers. We detect no change on these subsets, but the MMLU interval still admits a drop of 3.7 points.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Scored with the rule-based classifier instead, the edited column of Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> would be lower—0.273 rather than 0.380 on StrongREJECT, 0.340 rather than 0.480 on SimpleSafetyTests—because that classifier misses soft refusals containing no template phrase. We report the more conservative of the two judgments. Even so, the spread of the reduction, from 41 to 89 percentage points, is conspicuous. The two benchmarks with the highest residue, StrongREJECT and SimpleSafetyTests, are exactly the two whose content is concentrated in violence, sexual content, and self-harm. The two with the lowest, MaliciousInstruct and AdvBench, consist largely of requests for illegal procedures. What the single direction removed and what it left behind are therefore two questions to be answered separately.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Which Weights the Edit Needs</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The most direct way to find out how far the edit must reach is to bake nothing and instead attach lossless hooks to exactly the writers a bake stage would edit. The hooks subtract the direction’s component from their outputs at inference time. The hooks bypass quantization, so what they measure is the ceiling of the edit itself. A nested ladder (attention, then the dense and shared projections, then the routed experts) only ever measures what a group adds <em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">given</em> the groups before it, which depends on the order the ladder walks. We therefore measure all seven non-empty subsets of <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{</annotation></semantics></math>attention, dense, experts<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">}</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\}</annotation></semantics></math>, which makes the decomposition order-free. Evaluation uses 256 held-out harmful prompts, 164 from outside the AdvBench fitting slice and 92 from JailbreakBench, and pairs of conditions are compared by McNemar’s test on the same prompts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T7" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T7.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S5.T7.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T7.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Edited group</th>
<th id="S5.T7.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Judge</th>
<th id="S5.T7.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Removed</th>
<th id="S5.T7.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">Rule</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T7.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T7.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">none</th>
<td id="S5.T7.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.949</td>
<td id="S5.T7.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">—</td>
<td id="S5.T7.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.961</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T7.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T7.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">attention</th>
<td id="S5.T7.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.910</td>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>All seven writer-group subsets on 256 held-out harmful prompts. <em id="S5.T7.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Judge</em> counts <span id="S5.T7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span> only and is the primary metric; <em id="S5.T7.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Rule</em> is the opening-phrase classifier, which also counts unfinished replies. Judge rates are over 254–256 prompts, the remainder having no usable verdict. Against the unedited condition, attention is significant (11:1, <math id="S5.T7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.006" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.006</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.006</annotation></semantics></math>) and the routed experts are (39:1, <math id="S5.T7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=7{\times}10^{-11}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>11</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=7{\times}10^{-11}</annotation></semantics></math>); the dense group alone is not (6:2, <math id="S5.T7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.29" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.29</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.29</annotation></semantics></math>).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The groups are strongly non-additive</span> (Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 5.2 Which Weights the Edit Needs ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). Editing attention, the dense and shared projections, or the routed experts on their own removes 0.039, 0.016 and 0.148 of refusal; editing all three removes 0.776. The three single-group effects sum to 0.203, so 0.573, which is 74% of the joint effect, appears only when the groups are edited together. Editing the experts alone leaves refusal at 0.801; it is editing them together with the attention output projections that collapses it, to 0.408. The rule-based scoring gives the same picture with an interaction of 76% of the joint effect. What this establishes is a property of the intervention: the drop in refusal is strongly non-additive over writer groups. It does not by itself locate where refusal is represented, and we do not read it as such.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Attributing the joint effect to individual groups requires a convention. Shapley values, which split the interaction evenly over the orderings, give the experts 54%, attention 32% and the dense group 14% under the judge, and 53%, 30% and 17% under the rule classifier. We report them for completeness, with the seven raw subsets alongside, but with three quarters of the effect in the interaction term a Shapley share is an allocation rule applied to an intervention, not a statement about where refusal lives.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">What the numbers do support without a convention is the practical claim. The writers a name-matching implementation reaches on this model are exactly attention plus the dense and shared projections: 90 matrices at inference, whose removal takes refusal from 0.949 to 0.883. The 12,096 expert down-projections it does not reach are three-dimensional fused tensors whose names contain no “down projection” and fall outside the match; on disk the same gap covers 12,384 expert matrices, together with the token embedding, the MTP input projection and the vision merger, which the name match also misses. Editing what the recipe finds reports success and moves refusal by 0.066 out of an available 0.776. The failure is not that the architecture resists ablation but that the edit never touched most of the weights that matter; any implementation that enumerates the fused expert tensors avoids it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">One comparison is sensitive to the scorer. Adding the dense and shared projections on top of attention is not significant under the rule classifier (10:4, <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.18" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.18</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.18</annotation></semantics></math>) nor under the judge counting <span id="S5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span> only (12:5, <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.14" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.14</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.14</annotation></semantics></math>), but is significant when unfinished replies are counted as non-compliant (14:4, <math id="S5.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.031" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.031</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.031</annotation></semantics></math>). The dense group’s own contribution is small enough that which replies count as refusals determines whether it clears significance; we therefore report it as small and not established rather than as a null.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablation under a Multi-Stream Residual</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Manifold-constrained hyper-connections turn the residual into four streams, but every operation they perform on those streams is a scalar weighting per stream: a layer reads a scalar-weighted sum of the streams, writes its output back into them under scalar coefficients, and the <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> doubly stochastic mixing matrix between layers acts on the stream index rather than within the hidden dimension. All three operations multiply an entire <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector by a scalar and add, and orthogonality to <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> is preserved under scalar multiplication and addition. Hence if every writer’s output is orthogonal to <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, each of the four streams is orthogonal to <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, and so is any combination a layer reads. The premise of a single residual channel weakens to the requirement that the mixing operator does not rotate within the hidden dimension, and the conclusion survives. Tensor parallelism supplies a direct check: after the all-reduce, each layer’s residual is element-wise identical across the eight ranks, with a maximum difference of zero, so projecting per rank is consistent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">What the algebra settles is effectiveness. Equivalence with a projection at the layer boundary is a separate question, and we test it on the same 256 prompts and over the same layers, since the boundary probe registers a hook on every decoder layer, not on one, so what differs is where the projection is applied, not how much of the network it covers. On their own valid prompts the two conditions give 0.173 and 0.271 under the judge, and 0.156 and 0.223 under the rule classifier. The comparison itself is made on the 253 prompts with a usable verdict in both, where the rates are 0.174 and 0.265; those two ways of computing a rate differ by less than 0.01 here, but they are not the same quantity and we keep them apart. The marginal intervals overlap, so the difference is not visible in them; the paired test, which uses the per-prompt outcomes those intervals discard, finds it. Of 31 discordant pairs, 27 favor editing the writers (<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=3{\times}10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=3{\times}10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>); under the rule classifier it is 22 of 27 (<math id="S5.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p=0.0015" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.0015</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=0.0015</annotation></semantics></math>). The result holds under both scorers. The boundary projection may remove less because editing the writers takes the component out before it enters the residual, so no sublayer within the layer can read it, whereas projecting at the boundary leaves the feed-forward sublayer having already read an intermediate state containing <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, whose non-linear traces do not lie along <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> and cannot be projected away afterwards. Under hyper-connections a layer reads a combination of streams that already carries its own attention output, which would widen that exposure. But the same within-layer exposure exists in a single-stream Transformer, and this experiment cannot separate the two: it establishes that editing writers beats the boundary probe on this model, not that mHC is the reason.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>What the Edit Is Specific To</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A rank-one projection removes a direction from every residual writer, which is a substantial perturbation of the weights. Two questions follow: whether the drop in refusal is specific to <em id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">this</em> direction, and whether removing a second direction alongside it changes the outcome. We compare five conditions at layer 22 under hooks on all 132 writer sites, on 150 StrongREJECT and 100 JailbreakBench prompts (Table <a href="#S5.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 5.4 What the Edit Is Specific To ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>). The subspace is stored row-wise as <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> and applied as <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x-(xQ^{\top})Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x-(xQ^{\top})Q</annotation></semantics></math>, that is <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I-Q^{\top}Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I-Q^{\top}Q</annotation></semantics></math>; rows are orthonormalized by Gram–Schmidt with an explicit re-orthogonalization step, measuring <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.7\times 10^{-8}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.7\times 10^{-8}</annotation></semantics></math> between rows. The second direction is either the first principal component of the harmful-prompt residual deflated against the shipped direction, or a random unit vector orthogonal to it.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T8" class="ltx_table">

<tr id="S5.T8.2.2" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S5.T8.2.4" class="ltx_tr">

<tr id="S5.T8.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T8.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">random <math id="S5.T8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\perp r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>⟂</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\perp r</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="S5.T8.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">1</th>

<td id="S5.T8.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.920</td>
<td id="S5.T8.2.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">1.000</td>
<td id="S5.T8.2.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.960</td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T8.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T8.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><math id="S5.T8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r+\mathrm{PC}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>PC</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r+\mathrm{PC}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="S5.T8.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">2</th>

<th id="S5.T8.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><math id="S5.T8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r+\text{random}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>+</mo><mtext>random</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r+\text{random}</annotation></semantics></math></th>

<td id="S5.T8.2.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.253</td>
<td id="S5.T8.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">0.160</td>

</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Five ablation conditions at layer 22, all writers hooked, on 150 StrongREJECT (SR) and 100 JailbreakBench (JBB) prompts. <em id="S5.T8.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Judge</em> counts <span id="S5.T8.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span> only and is the primary metric; <em id="S5.T8.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Rule</em> is the opening-phrase classifier. Each condition leaves between <math id="S5.T8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1{\times}10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1{\times}10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.T8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5{\times}10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5{\times}10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> of every ablated direction in the residual, so no condition is an inert hook.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The effect is specific to the direction removed.</span> Ablating a random direction orthogonal to <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> leaves refusal at 0.987 and 0.920, indistinguishable from the unedited 0.993 and 0.920, while ablating <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> leaves 0.320 and 0.190. Projecting <em id="S5.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">something</em> out of every residual writer does not loosen the model. One random direction is one control. It shows that this particular arbitrary direction does nothing; several independent draws would be needed to say the same of arbitrary directions in general.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Neither of the two tested rank-2 extensions restored refusal: 0.307 and 0.253 on StrongREJECT against 0.320 for rank 1. We did not run the paired comparison that would be needed to say whether either improves on rank 1.</p>
</div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span>Residual refusal of the edited model by content category, counting only <span id="S5.T9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, with Wilson 95% confidence intervals. The rows sum to the benchmark totals in Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>: 57 of 150 on StrongREJECT and 25 of 150 on HarmBench.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The refusal that survives the edit is not spread evenly. Table <a href="#S5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ 5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> breaks the residue down by content category on StrongREJECT and HarmBench, whose taxonomies differ. All six StrongREJECT categories sit at 0.96–1.00 on the base model; after editing, violence leaves a residue of 0.62, sexual content 0.50, and hate and harassment 0.48, against 0.15 for illegal goods and 0.21 for non-violent crimes. On HarmBench, harassment and bullying leave 0.27 and chemical/biological 0.16, against 0.00 for cybercrime and 0.07 for misinformation. The category names differ but the pattern repeats: requests about physical harm, sex, and hate resist the edit, while requests about illegal procedures and technical intrusion are almost entirely released. This is where the spread across benchmarks in Table <a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.1 Main Results ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> comes from, since StrongREJECT and SimpleSafetyTests are filled with content of the first kind.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Coverage within the model as it runs is not the explanation: the hook experiment of Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 5.2 Which Weights the Edit Needs ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> attaches to every residual writer on the inference path—all 132 sites, covering the 12,186 matrices the loaded model exercises—and the residue is there all the same. It is not quantization loss: the hook experiment bypasses quantization. What remains is that these categories might be carried by a different direction, or by a subspace of low rank. We tested that by fitting subspaces on prompts from violence, sexual content and hate alone—81 for fitting, 73 disjoint for evaluation—at every rank from 1 to 12 (Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>).</p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T10.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">6</td>

<tr id="S5.T10.2.13" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T10.2.13.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;">11</td>

</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>Subspaces fitted on the resistant categories alone, evaluated on 73 held-out prompts from the same categories. <em id="S5.T10.8" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Judge</em> counts <span id="S5.T10.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span> only over the <math id="S5.T10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> prompts with a usable verdict; <em id="S5.T10.10" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Rule</em> is the opening-phrase classifier over all 73; <em id="S5.T10.11" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Unfinished</em> is the share of the 73 the judge labelled <span id="S5.T10.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span>. The ranks are independently fitted rather than nested: the first row of every subspace is the deterministic difference of means, but rows beyond it come from a randomized SVD with no fixed per-call seed, so differences between ranks carry fitting randomness as well as rank.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Every rank removes most of this refusal, from 0.986 down to between 0.20 and 0.47, and none removes it. The two scorers do not agree on which rank does best: the judge’s lowest value is 0.200 at rank 8 (<math id="S5.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="14/70" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>14</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>70</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">14/70</annotation></semantics></math>, Wilson <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.123,0.308]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.123</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.308</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.123,0.308]</annotation></semantics></math>), the rule classifier’s is 0.219 at rank 3. The intervals are wide and mostly overlapping—rank 3 under the judge is <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="17/73=0.233" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>17</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>73</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.233</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17/73=0.233</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.151,0.342]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.151</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.342</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.151,0.342]</annotation></semantics></math>—though not uniformly so: rank 5 at <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.466" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.466</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.466</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S5.SS5.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.356,0.579]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0.356</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.579</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.356,0.579]</annotation></semantics></math>, is separated from both. With twelve conditions on 73 prompts, subspaces fitted independently at each rank, and a minimum selected after the fact, these data do not identify a best rank. They do show a residue that none of the twelve edits removed, on a set of categories where the same class of edit removes the bulk of refusal elsewhere.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The unfinished column is reported alongside the residue because it does not stay constant: it rises from 0.027 at rank 1 to 0.205 at rank 10. Under a fixed 384-token budget, higher-rank edits leave more replies unfinished, and a <span id="S5.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>-only rate falls mechanically when replies stop arriving at an answer. The judge’s lowest value, 0.200 at rank 8, sits where 0.164 of replies did not finish, so that value mixes refusal removed with answers never reached. We did not inspect the outputs; what we report is a falling completion rate under a fixed budget.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Ethics and Responsible Release</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Threat model.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The attack used here is not new. The directional-ablation recipe was published with an implementation in 2024 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arditi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, the base model’s weights are released under the MIT license, and the edited checkpoint we study is itself already public. What an open release does and does not change about marginal risk is itself contested <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. What an attacker needs is the weights, eight H100s, roughly five minutes of disk writes, and a few hundred harmful prompts. All of that was available before this paper. What we add is measurement rather than capability: the reach of this attack on a frontier-scale architecture, and where it stops. We do publish engineering detail an attacker could use: that the writers have to be enumerated structurally, how many requantization iterations the block-FP8 format needs, and that distributed generation must keep every rank in the same decode loop. That detail lowers the engineering uncertainty of reproducing the attack, though not its cost in compute or data, and it is the same detail a defender needs to audit the weights that matter. The paper is not cost-neutral for an attacker; we argue that the balance favors the defender, for the reasons below.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">What defenders gain.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The measurements in §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Which Weights the Edit Needs ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> and §<a href="#S5.SS5" title="5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.5</span></a> were made against an attack, but two of them bear directly on defense. One is the blind spot: an audit that enumerates residual writers by module name covers 0.7% of those on the inference path and reports no error, so the same traversal that makes the attack fail silently would make a defense fail silently, and the fix is the same in both directions — enumerate by tensor structure. The other is the residue. A form of refusal survived every subspace we fitted on the categories it concentrates in, which is the one positive result here a defender can build on, though what carries it is unknown and hardening one writer group may run into the same non-additivity the attack did.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Release conditions.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The edited weights and the model card were already published,<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://huggingface.co/orcarouter/GLM-5.3-Flash-Uncensored-FP8" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/orcarouter/GLM-5.3-Flash-Uncensored-FP8</a></span></span></span> under the same license as the base model, and this paper does not change that. What we do not release with the paper is the implementation: the enumeration of writers, the iterated orthogonalization on block-FP8 weights, and the per-shard baking scripts. The two differ in kind: the published weights are one specific checkpoint, whereas the implementation is a general tool that applies to any mixture-of-experts checkpoint. It is the latter that adds leverage for an attacker. We likewise do not release the fitted refusal direction, the subspaces fitted on the resistant categories, or the prompt slices used to fit them. The category names are published, because they are part of the finding itself: knowing which content resists this class of attack is useful to a defender, and knowing it does not help an attacker remove it. This trade-off has a cost, which we state in the limitations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Implications for safety in the weights.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A rank-one edit that involves no training removes between 41 and 89 percentage points of this model’s refusal. The reduction is consistent with a low-dimensional component of refusal that can be altered without a detectable change on the four capability benchmarks tested here, which is what makes refusal and capability look separable. Separability of that kind would be bad news for defenders: what is separable can be excised on its own. The same experiments supply the other half of the picture. The refusal that resists was not removed by any of the twelve subspaces we fitted on those categories; it ships with the weights and survived every edit we tried.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Research program.</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work is part of OrcaRouter Research,<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://www.orcarouter.ai" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://www.orcarouter.ai</a></span></span></span> an effort to study the security properties of frontier AI systems and the infrastructure used to deploy them. We are particularly interested in the boundary between model-level safety mechanisms and system-level security controls: which properties can be reliably enforced in model weights, which can be altered by an adversary with weight access, and which therefore require enforcement at the inference and agent-infrastructure layers. The measurements reported here fall on both sides of that boundary. Most of this model’s refusal was removable from the weights by an edit that needs no training, which places it among the properties an operator cannot rely on the weights alone to hold; the fraction that resisted every edit we tried is a property this study cannot yet assign to either side.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We applied an unmodified single-direction ablation recipe to a sparse mixture-of-experts model of roughly 320B parameters, with 288 routed experts per layer, a residual carried by four parallel streams, and weights released in block-FP8. The recipe itself was left alone. The direction is still the difference of means of the last-token representation over harmful and harmless prompts, and the edit is still one rank-one projection of the weights that write the residual stream, with no training, no gradients, and no second direction. Applying it to this model took three pieces of handling, each of which we measured the cost of. Writers are enumerated by tensor structure rather than by module name, giving 12,479 matrices, of which 12,384 are expert down-projections inside fused tensors; 12,442 of them are stored in FP8 and 37 in BF16. Activations are collapsed under the hyper-connection mixing weights before the representation is taken. Orthogonalization on quantized weights is done iteratively: 32 iterations bring the residual leakage from 13.4% down to 5.2% and the baked refusal rate from 0.188 to 0.094, against a lossless-hook prediction of 0.031.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The edited model’s refusal rate on the seven harmful benchmarks falls from 0.51–1.00 to 0.08–0.48, every reduction is significant under a paired test, and across nearly 800 harmful prompts only two run the other way. The four capability scores move by no more than 1.0 point, three up and one down. False refusal on harmless prompts falls, from 0.024 to zero. The direction was fitted on 256 AdvBench prompts alone, and the clean variants that exclude the fitting sample give the same reduction as the originals, so what was removed is not memorization of that sample.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The anatomy comes from four further analyses. Editing attention, the dense and shared projections, or the routed experts on their own removes 0.039, 0.016 and 0.148 of refusal, while editing all three removes 0.776: three quarters of the effect exists only in the joint intervention. Matching module names reaches 0.7% of the writers on the inference path, and editing them moves refusal by 0.066 out of 0.776 without raising an error. The multi-stream residual does not obstruct ablation, because its cross-stream mixing weights each stream by a scalar and performs no rotation within the hidden dimension. Editing the writers is nonetheless more thorough than projecting at the layer boundary over the same layers, 0.174 against 0.265 on the prompts valid in both conditions, a difference the marginal intervals hide and the paired test finds. What the edit removes is specific to the direction removed: a random direction orthogonal to it leaves refusal unchanged, and neither of the two rank-2 extensions we tested restored it. On violence, sexual content and hate, subspaces fitted specifically on those categories bring the residue from 0.986 to between 0.20 and 0.47, and none of the twelve ranks removes it.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A single direction reaches most of this model’s refusal, but only when it is projected out of all of the writers at once. It survived two architectural changes: fused expert tensors require only a different way of enumerating the writers, and a multi-stream residual requires only that the mixing operator not rotate within the hidden dimension. Residual refusal remains concentrated in a few content categories. The scope should be stated plainly: one model, one selected layer for direction estimation, and the intervention procedures tested here. Whether it generalizes to other frontier mixture-of-experts models, and what carries the refusal that resists, remain unmeasured.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A single model.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every result comes from GLM-5.3-Flash, with no cross-vendor comparison. The architecture-dependent conclusions—that fused expert tensors must be enumerated structurally, and that per-stream scalar mixing preserves orthogonality—transfer to models with the same features. The specific numbers, including the size of the interaction term, the choice of layer 22, and the per-category residues, are properties of this one checkpoint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Judgment depends on a model.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Refusal is judged by a judge model, with no human annotation. The judge and the rule-based classifier agree on 0.85–0.96 of responses on the harmful benchmarks, and the disagreement runs systematically toward the rule underestimating refusal. For small effects such as false refusal we rely on an improved judge prompt rather than an independent human check.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The two scorers disagree unevenly across conditions.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every experiment reported here is scored by both the judge model and the rule-based classifier; 5,475 hook-experiment responses were re-judged alongside the main results. The disagreement between them is not a constant offset: on the writer-subset sweep the rule classifier reads higher than the judge on lightly edited conditions and lower on heavily edited ones, by up to 0.048 in either direction. Because the two conventions also differ in how they treat unfinished replies, a comparison whose margin is small can change significance with the convention, as the dense group’s increment does. We report both scorers wherever a comparison is close.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Capability evaluation is a subset.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each of the four benchmarks is sampled down to a few hundred items, which rules out a large regression but does not substitute for a full evaluation harness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The rank sweep is exploratory.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The twelve subspaces were fitted independently rather than as one nested basis (Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>), so the sweep compares twelve independently fitted subspaces and does not measure what one more dimension does. Selecting the minimum over twelve conditions on 73 evaluation prompts compounds that. A controlled version would fix the seed, nest the bases, and pre-register the comparison.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">One random control, no power analysis.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The direction-specificity result rests on a single random orthogonal direction; several would be needed to rule out arbitrary-direction explanations in general. The capability comparison reports paired intervals but no power analysis, so we quote no minimum detectable effect. Thinking mode is untested: all evaluation runs at <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">reasoning_effort=low</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rates carry run-to-run variation.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Greedy decoding under tensor parallelism is not bit-deterministic. Two runs of the same condition on the same prompts with the same seed gave base refusal rates of 0.949 and 0.961, so a rate carries roughly 1–3 points of run-to-run noise. Every comparison we report is made within a single run, and we make no claim about differences of a few points across runs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Withholding the implementation has a cost.</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We do not publish the code for the editing pipeline, so verification rests entirely on the description in the method section. We give there everything an independent implementation needs—the full writer inventory and the criterion defining it, the iteration count against residual leakage, the two ways the scales must be handled, and the three reasons the rewrite has to proceed shard by shard—but that is not the same as reproducing by download, and a reader has to invest engineering effort to rebuild it.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Judge label counts</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Every rate in this paper comes from a judge model that assigns each response one of three
labels—<span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span>, or <span id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span> for a reply that ran
out of the token budget before answering—or, rarely, no usable label after retries. The
main text counts a response as a refusal when and only when the label is <span id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">That choice matters, so the counts behind it are given here. From them a reader can
recompute any rate under a different convention, see exactly which denominators shrank
where a verdict is missing, and check the two places where the convention changes the
answer. Column <span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">r</span> is <span id="A1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, <span id="A1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">c</span> is <span id="A1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span>, <span id="A1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">u</span>
is <span id="A1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span>, and <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math> counts responses with no usable label.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Worked example, HarmBench in Table <a href="#A1.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix A Judge label counts ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>: the base model gives 138
<span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>, 5 <span id="A1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span> and 7 <span id="A1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span> over 150 prompts. The main
table reports <math id="A1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="138/150=0.920" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>138</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.920</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">138/150=0.920</annotation></semantics></math>. Counting anything that is not <span id="A1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span> as a
refusal would give <math id="A1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="145/150=0.967" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>145</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.967</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">145/150=0.967</annotation></semantics></math> instead.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T11" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T11.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A1.T11.2.1" class="ltx_tr">

<th id="A1.T11.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;" colspan="4">Base</th>
<th id="A1.T11.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;" colspan="4">Edited</th></tr>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>Labels behind Table <a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 5.2 Which Weights the Edit Needs ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. The harmless columns are the first place the
convention decides the answer: the unedited model refuses 5 of 100 harmless prompts, but 21
more replies run past the token budget, so counting non-<span id="A1.T12.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">compliance</span> as refusal would
report a false-refusal rate of 0.260 for a model whose false-refusal rate is 0.050. The
sweep’s 3,276 records are these nine conditions over 256 harmful, 100 harmless and 8
quarantined prompts, the last being prompts inside the fitting slice, scored separately.</figcaption>

<th id="A1.T13.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;" colspan="4">JBB (100)</th></tr>

<td id="A1.T14.2.12.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">15</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.12.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">0</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T14.2.13" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T14.2.13.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">11</th>
<td id="A1.T14.2.13.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">20</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.13.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">42</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.13.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">11</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.13.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">0</td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T14.2.14" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A1.T14.2.14.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">12</th>
<td id="A1.T14.2.14.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">16</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.14.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">44</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.14.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">13</td>
<td id="A1.T14.2.14.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:5.0pt;padding-right:5.0pt;">0</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 14: </span>Labels behind Table <a href="#S5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ 5.5 What Resists ‣ 5 Results ‣ How Fragile Is Safety Alignment at Frontier Scale? A Single-Direction Attack on a 320B MoE" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>, 73 prompts per rank. This is the second
place the convention decides the answer. Ranks 6, 7 and 8 lose 3, 2 and 3 responses to
missing labels, which is why their denominators are 70, 71 and 70 rather than 73, and
<span id="A1.T14.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">unfinished</span> climbs from 2 at rank 1 to 15 at rank 10—so a low
<span id="A1.T14.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">refusal</span>-only rate at high rank is partly replies that never reached an answer.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These tables cover 8,259 response records: 2,784 for the main results (both checkpoints over
eleven benchmark sections), 3,276 for the writer-subset sweep, 1,250 for the direction
conditions and 949 for the rank sweep. The number of judge calls is smaller, because verdicts
are cached on the prompt and the response together and two conditions that produce identical
text for the same prompt are judged once; every record carries a label either way.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
